To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the presence of a chronic spinal cord injury (SCI) is associated with a lower incidence of intraoperative spinal cord monitoring (IOM) abnormalities in patients who undergo surgery for acute cervical SCI.

the intraoperative somatosensy evoked potential (SSEP) findings are not reliable for predicting the severity of acute spinal canal compromise in patients with cervical spondylosis and spinal stenosis.
the use of the intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring in the form of somatosensory cortical evoked potentials (SSEPs) is a reliable method to monitor the spinal canal during spinal surgery.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of a novel, low cost, and easy to implement, non-invasive, and portable system for the measurement of the somatosensory-evoked potentials (SSEP).
the use of a new method for the detection of spinal cord ischemia in patients with acute and chronic spinal cord compression.
the development of a novel and highly sensitive method to determine the mechanical properties of single living cells, based on optical tweezers and fluorescence microscopy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results of intraoperative SSEPs are not predictive of the outcome of the patient with a spinal cord injury.
the use of SSEPs is a safe and effective method of intraoperative monitoring in patients undergoing spine surgeries.
the use of SSEP monitoring is an essential part of spinal surgery, especially when the spinal cord is exposed and the dura is opened.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of intraoperative somatosensors evoked potential (SEP) monitoring in patients with chronic or acute spinal canal compromise is a valuable tool to prevent and detect neurological injury.
the spinal canal is a very important anatomical structure and that it can be compromised acutely or chronically.
the spinal cord is more susceptible to ischemia than the peripheral nerves.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of intraoperative neuromonitoring in spine surgery can reduce the incidence of new postoperative neurological deficit.
the spinal cord is more vulnerable to ischemic damage than the peripheral nerve.
there is a need for more research into the relationship between the spinal cord and the brain, especially in the context of spinal cord injuries.
